```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse   = TRUE,
  comment    = "#>",
  fig.width  = 6,
  fig.height = 5,
  dpi        = 110
)
```

```{r}
library(BiHeat)

set.seed(1)
species   <- LETTERS[1:6]
sites     <- letters[1:8]
observed  <- matrix(runif(48), 6, 8, dimnames = list(species, sites))
predicted <- observed + matrix(rnorm(48, sd = 0.15), 6, 8,
                               dimnames = list(species, sites))
```

Every option on this page is an argument to `incubate()`. `biheat()` forwards
its `...` to the same place, and `plot()` accepts them as a final pass, so the
three forms below are interchangeable and this vignette mixes them freely.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
biheat(observed, predicted, cell_inset = 0.1)
breed(observed, predicted) |> incubate(cell_inset = 0.1) |> plot()
breed(observed, predicted) |> plot(cell_inset = 0.1)
```

## Palettes

The two triangles carry two gradients. `palettes()` bundles them, taking a
character vector of two or more colours per side, which
`scales::gradient_n_pal()` interpolates across.

```{r}
palettes(c("white", "darkorange", "darkred"),
         c("white", "steelblue", "navy"))
```

```{r}
biheat(observed, predicted,
       palettes = palettes(c("white", "darkorange", "darkred"),
                           c("white", "steelblue", "navy")))
```

A bare character vector is read as the upper palette, with `lower_palette` as
its companion, which saves a call when both sides are simple ramps:

```{r}
biheat(observed, predicted,
       palettes = c("grey95", "forestgreen"),
       lower_palette = c("grey95", "purple4"))
```

Three or more stops give a diverging ramp, which suits a matrix centred on
zero. Residuals are the usual case:

```{r}
residual <- predicted - observed
biheat(observed, residual,
       upper_name = "observed",
       lower_name = "residual",
       palettes = palettes(c("white", "grey20"),
                           c("steelblue", "white", "firebrick")))
```

The colour a value lands on depends on the range the palette is stretched
across, which `scale` controls. `vignette("biheat")` covers the choice between
`"separate"` and `"shared"`.

### Choosing a pair

Two properties matter more here than in a single-scale heatmap, because the two
palettes have to be told apart inside one cell.

The two hues need to stay separable. The default red and blue remain
distinguishable under the common red-green colour deficiencies, and a green
paired with a red does not. Orange with purple, and green with purple, both hold
up as alternatives.

Both ramps should start from a similar lightness. Anchoring each at white or a
pale grey means a cell whose halves are both pale reads as two low values rather
than as one low value beside a differently coloured one, and the split stays
visible only where it carries information.

```{r}
biheat(observed, predicted,
       palettes = palettes(c("grey97", "#E66100"),
                           c("grey97", "#5D3A9B")))
```

Ramps that start dark work when the panel is dense enough that pale cells would
disappear, at the cost of making low values the loudest thing in the figure.

## Printing the values

`show_values = TRUE` writes each number inside its own triangle, at two
significant digits:

```{r}
biheat(observed[, 1:5], predicted[, 1:5], show_values = TRUE)
```

Labels are sized in millimetres by `value_size`, the same unit
`ggplot2::geom_text()` uses. The default of 3 suits a panel of roughly this
size; a denser grid needs a smaller number, and the labels start to collide
somewhere past 10 columns at the default figure width.

```{r}
biheat(observed, predicted, show_values = TRUE, value_size = 2.1)
```

## Cell geometry

`cell_inset` shrinks every cell on all four sides, as a fraction of its width
and height. The default of `0.04` leaves a thin gap that keeps neighbouring
cells legible. `0` makes the grid contiguous:

```{r}
biheat(observed, predicted, cell_inset = 0)
```

Larger values pull the cells apart, which reads well when the individual
comparison matters more than the pattern across the panel:

```{r}
biheat(observed, predicted, cell_inset = 0.15)
```

The argument accepts anything in `[0, 0.5)`, and `0.5` would shrink a cell to
nothing.

Outlines are separate from the gap. `grid_colour` draws a border around each
triangle and `grid_linewidth` sets its weight, so a contiguous grid can still
show its cut lines:

```{r}
biheat(observed, predicted,
       cell_inset = 0,
       grid_colour = "white",
       grid_linewidth = 0.6)
```

Both default to nothing drawn (`NA` colour at width `0`). Outlining every
triangle on a large matrix costs legibility, so a fine linewidth pays off past
a few hundred cells.

## Missing cells

A cell missing a value on one side keeps its other half, and the gap takes
`na_colour`:

```{r}
observed_gaps <- observed
observed_gaps[2, 3] <- NA
observed_gaps[5, 7] <- NA
observed_gaps[1, 1] <- NA

biheat(observed_gaps, predicted, na_colour = "grey80")
```

The default is `"grey90"`. Something further from the palettes in use makes an
absent value harder to misread as a low one, which matters most when a palette
starts at white.

## Skewed values

Each palette is stretched linearly across its range, so one extreme value
compresses everything else into the pale end. A matrix of counts usually has
this shape:

```{r}
set.seed(7)
counts <- matrix(rpois(48, lambda = 3), 6, 8,
                 dimnames = list(species, sites))
counts[2, 4] <- 180

expected <- matrix(rpois(48, lambda = 3), 6, 8,
                   dimnames = list(species, sites))
expected[2, 4] <- 150

biheat(counts, expected)
```

One cell holds the top of both scales and the other 47 sit near the bottom.
BiHeat has no transform argument, since transforming the matrix before
`breed()` does the job and keeps what was plotted explicit:

```{r}
biheat(log1p(counts), log1p(expected),
       upper_name = "log1p(counts)",
       lower_name = "log1p(expected)")
```

Ranking is the other option when only the ordering matters, and it puts both
matrices on the same bounded scale as a side effect:

```{r}
rank_matrix <- function(m) {
  out <- matrix(rank(m, na.last = "keep"), nrow(m), ncol(m),
                dimnames = dimnames(m))
  out / max(out, na.rm = TRUE)
}

biheat(rank_matrix(counts), rank_matrix(expected),
       scale = "shared",
       upper_name = "counts (rank)",
       lower_name = "expected (rank)")
```

The colourbar labels report the transformed numbers under either approach, which
is why both examples above set `upper_name` and `lower_name` to say so.

## Ordering rows and columns

Rows are drawn top to bottom and columns left to right, in the order they carry
after `breed()` aligned them. `row_order` and `col_order` take a permutation of
those labels and rearrange the panel.

Sorting by something computed from the data is the useful case. Here the
species with the largest mean absolute error move to the top:

```{r}
cells <- comes_out(breed(observed, predicted))
mae_by_species <- tapply(abs(cells$upper - cells$lower), cells$row, mean)
worst_first <- names(sort(mae_by_species, decreasing = TRUE))
round(sort(mae_by_species, decreasing = TRUE), 3)
```

```{r}
biheat(observed, predicted, row_order = worst_first)
```

Column order works the same way, and the two combine:

```{r}
site_totals <- colMeans(observed)
biheat(observed, predicted,
       row_order = worst_first,
       col_order = names(sort(site_totals, decreasing = TRUE)))
```

Both arguments require a full permutation of the labels, so a partial vector
stops the call and every row stays in the panel:

```{r, error = TRUE}
biheat(observed, predicted, row_order = c("A", "B"))
```

## The legend

`legend_position` takes `"right"` (the default), `"bottom"`, or `"none"`.
`legend_orientation` controls whether the two colourbars stack or sit side by
side.

```{r, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5.5}
biheat(observed, predicted,
       legend_position = "bottom",
       legend_orientation = "horizontal")
```

Below the two bars sits the key glyph: a split tile showing which triangle
belongs to which name, with a callout to each. It follows the `split` setting,
so it always matches the diagonal drawn in the panel. `show_key = FALSE` drops
it, which is worth doing for a small multiple where the same key would repeat:

```{r, fig.height = 4}
biheat(observed, predicted, show_key = FALSE)
```

Dropping the key also changes the return type. With no glyph to inject, the
underlying ggplot comes back rather than a gtable, and that object accepts
ggplot2's `+`:

```{r, fig.height = 4}
biheat(observed, predicted, show_key = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

`legend_position = "none"` removes the legend and the key together.

`bi_legend()` builds the same paired legend as a standalone grob, for figures
where the panel is assembled somewhere else:

```{r, fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 3}
grid::grid.draw(
  bi_legend("observed", "predicted",
            upper_range = range(observed),
            lower_range = range(predicted),
            split = "down")
)
```

Its ranges are yours to supply, so a legend can be shared across several panels
by passing the pooled range to all of them.

## Titles and axis labels

`title`, `subtitle`, and `caption` behave the way they do anywhere in ggplot2.
`theme_biheat()` centres the first two and italicises the caption:

```{r}
biheat(observed, predicted,
       title = "Occurrence probability",
       subtitle = "field survey against model fit",
       caption = "6 species x 8 sites")
```

Axis titles are blank by default, since the tick labels usually name the axis
on their own. Supplying `xlab` or `ylab` switches that axis title back on:

```{r}
biheat(observed, predicted, xlab = "site", ylab = "species")
```

`upper_name` and `lower_name` override the labels on the colourbars and in the
key glyph. `breed()` reads them from the symbols you passed, so they only need
setting when the variable names are unhelpful:

```{r, fig.height = 4}
biheat(observed, predicted,
       upper_name = "field survey",
       lower_name = "model fit",
       show_key = FALSE)
```

## The theme

`theme_biheat()` is a `ggplot2::theme_minimal()` with the panel grid,
background, axis ticks, and axis titles removed, tick labels laid horizontally,
and the legend keyed to the left. It is applied for you inside `plot()`, and
exported for use with `geom_biheat()`.

`base_size` scales the whole thing:

```{r, fig.height = 4}
library(ggplot2)

cells$site    <- factor(cells$col, levels = sites)
cells$species <- factor(cells$row, levels = rev(species))

ggplot(cells, aes(site, species, upper = upper, lower = lower)) +
  geom_biheat() +
  theme_biheat(base_size = 15)
```

`base` swaps the theme underneath, which keeps the heatmap adjustments while
changing everything else:

```{r, fig.height = 4}
ggplot(cells, aes(site, species, upper = upper, lower = lower)) +
  geom_biheat() +
  theme_biheat(base = theme_dark(base_size = 11))
```

## Keeping a set of figures consistent

Several BiHeat panels in one document need the same options, and the readable
way to do that is a configured clutch rather than a repeated argument list.
`incubate()` is additive, so a shared configuration can be applied first and
the per-figure options added after:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
house_style <- function(clutch) {
  incubate(clutch,
           palettes = palettes(c("grey97", "#E66100"),
                               c("grey97", "#5D3A9B")),
           cell_inset = 0.06,
           legend_position = "bottom",
           legend_orientation = "horizontal")
}

house_style(breed(observed, predicted)) |> plot(title = "Panel A")
house_style(breed(observed, residual))  |> plot(title = "Panel B")
```

Colours only mean the same thing across panels if the ranges match, and
`scale = "shared"` shares a range between the two triangles of one figure
rather than across figures. Matching across figures means fixing the range
yourself, which the clutch route does not expose; `geom_biheat()` takes
`upper_range` and `lower_range` for exactly this, and
`vignette("geom-biheat")` covers it.

## Saving

`ggplot2::ggsave()` accepts a `biheat_plot` gtable as it does a ggplot:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
p <- biheat(observed, predicted, title = "Occurrence probability")
ggplot2::ggsave("biheat.png", p, width = 7, height = 5.5, dpi = 300)
ggplot2::ggsave("biheat.pdf", p, width = 7, height = 5.5)
```

Give the figure room. The legend column holds two colourbars and the key glyph
at fixed centimetre sizes, so a width under about 5 inches squeezes the panel
rather than the legend. Moving the legend to the bottom buys back the width.
